title: Neonatal and child mortality by mothers’ ethnic group and socio-economic status
meta_description: Article summarising findings from ONS analysis of the risk of neonatal and child mortality by mothers' ethnic group and household socio-economic status

breadcrumb.text: Neonatal and child mortality by mothers’ ethnic group and socio-economic status

lede: Babies born to Asian/Asian British Pakistani mothers saw the highest risk of neonatal and child death

body.text: 5 June 2024

body.alt: graphic showing hospital and health centre with icons of people and a person holding a baby

body.box_text:
This article uses data on self-reported ethnic group from the 2011 Census. We've grouped some of the response options together, and shortened some of the labels, for simplicity.

A full table of the abbreviations we've used is available in the [Glossary](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/childhealth/articles/neonatalandchildmortalitybymothersethnicgroupandsocioeconomicstatus/2024-06-05#glossary).

body.text: This article explains findings from ONS research into inequalities in neonatal and child mortality in England and Wales, using information from birth registrations, 2011 Census data and death registrations.

If you are affected by the issues in this article, you can find information about where to seek help in the [Help with issues raised in this article](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/childhealth/articles/neonatalandchildmortalitybymothersethnicgroupandsocioeconomicstatus/2024-06-05#help-with-issues-raised-in-this-article) section.

body.h2: What is child mortality?
body.text: What is child mortality?

body.h2: What is child mortality?
body.text: Child mortality is a measure of the proportion of babies who die before reaching later childhood. It is commonly used as an indicator of population health.

body.h2: What is child mortality?
body.text: Overall, child mortality in England and Wales has been reducing since the 1980s. [In 2022, around 3.9 in every 1,000 infants died before their first birthday](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/bulletins/childhoodinfantandperinatalmortalityinenglandandwales/2022).

body.h2: What is child mortality?
body.text: However, improvements to the child mortality rate have slowed in recent years. [The UK has some of the highest child mortality rates in Europe](https://www.bmj.com/content/368/bmj.m849), so it’s important to understand as much as we can about current trends.

body.h2: What is child mortality?
body.text: In this article, we have followed a cohort of children born between 2011 and 2016, until December 2021, when the oldest children in the cohort were aged 10 years.

body.h2: What is child mortality?
body.text: First, we looked at how neonatal and child mortality rates differed depending on the birth mothers’ ethnic group or the socio-economic status of adults in the household, using an occupation-based measure called [National Statistics Socio-economic Classification (NS-SEC)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/classificationsandstandards/otherclassifications/thenationalstatisticssocioeconomicclassificationnssecrebasedonsoc2010).

body.h2: What is child mortality?
body.text: We then estimated risk of death in our cohort, using statistical modelling.

body.h2: What is child mortality?
body.text: We have looked at neonatal mortality (from birth up to 28 days) and child mortality (after 28 days) separately, as the risk of death and causes of death are very different for these two groups.

body.h2: Mortality rates were highest for babies born to Pakistani mothers and those in out-of-work households
body.text: Mortality rates were highest for babies born to Pakistani mothers and those in out-of-work households

body.h2: Mortality rates were highest for babies born to Pakistani mothers and those in out-of-work households
body.text: Our analysis included 3 million babies born between Census Day 2011 (27 March 2011) and 31 December 2016. Further information on our study population is available in the [Measuring the data](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/childhealth/articles/neonatalandchildmortalitybymothersethnicgroupandsocioeconomicstatus/2024-06-05#measuring-the-data) section.

body.h2: Mortality rates were highest for babies born to Pakistani mothers and those in out-of-work households
body.text: In total, there were 9,955 deaths in our follow-up period 4,750 (48%) of which occurred in the neonatal period (within 28 days of birth).

body.h2: Mortality rates were highest for babies born to Pakistani mothers and those in out-of-work households
body.text: We measure mortality rates using a standard measure that compares the number of deaths to the years of life lived, called deaths per 1,000 child-years. This takes into account both the number of children in the cohort, and the follow-up time.

body.h2: Mortality rates were highest for babies born to Pakistani mothers and those in out-of-work households
body.text: Babies born to Pakistani mothers had the highest rate of neonatal and child mortality, at 45.8 per 1,000 child-years and 0.8 per 1,000 child-years, respectively. This is an estimate that falls within a range; [confidence intervals](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/childhealth/articles/neonatalandchildmortalitybymothersethnicgroupandsocioeconomicstatus/2024-06-05#glossary) for all estimates are available in the [associated data tables](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/childhealth/articles/neonatalandchildmortalitybymothersethnicgroupandsocioeconomicstatus/2024-06-05#related-data).

body.h2: Mortality rates were highest for babies born to Pakistani mothers and those in out-of-work households
body.text: Meanwhile, neonatal and child mortality rates were lowest in the White Other group (15.9 per 1,000 child-years and 0.2 per 1,000 child-years, respectively).

body.h2: Mortality rates were highest for babies born to Pakistani mothers and those in out-of-work households
body.text: When comparing rates by socio-economic status, households where the main earner had never worked or was long-term unemployed had the highest rates of neonatal and child deaths (31.9 per 1,000 child-years and 0.6 per 1,000 child-years, respectively).

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: We used statistical techniques to estimate inequalities in child mortality and understand which factors are most closely associated with the differences between ethnic groups and people of different socio-economic status.

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: First, we used a statistical model to estimate the difference in risk for babies born to mothers of different ethnic groups and socio-economic status (Model 1). This accounted for differences in the average age of mothers between groups and the babies’ sex. This is because we know that these factors play an important role in the risk of death.

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: A second model helped us understand the extent to which the differences in mortality between ethnic groups and socio-economic statuses found in Model 1 were related to other characteristics.

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: Our second model (Model 2) accounted for differences in household characteristics like mother’s country of birth, and babies’ (gestational) characteristics, including premature birth and suspected congenital abnormalities.

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: When looking at ethnicity, we also accounted for socio-economic status, and when looking at socio-economic status, we adjusted for ethnicity. We’ve provided further information about the models in the [Measuring the data](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/childhealth/articles/neonatalandchildmortalitybymothersethnicgroupandsocioeconomicstatus/2024-06-05#measuring-the-data) section.

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: If there is a big difference in the estimated relative risks between models, this means that the factors accounted for in Model 2 are influencing the estimated risk of death seen in that group.

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: It’s important to understand that the following figures reflect estimated risk based on a statistical model, accounting for multiple factors simultaneously, rather than actual mortality for children in our cohort.

body.h2: Understanding the differences in child mortality by ethnic group and socio-economic status
body.text: These estimates tell us about statistical relationships between neonatal and child mortality and belonging to a certain ethnic or socio-economic group, but we cannot say what is causing these differences.

This reflects the trends seen in the overall mortality rates.

body.h2: Risk of both neonatal and child death was higher in households with long-term unemployment
body.text: Risk of both neonatal and child death was higher in households with long-term unemployment

body.h2: Risk of both neonatal and child death was higher in households with long-term unemployment
body.text: We also compared mortality risk for babies and children based on the socio-economic status of the adults in their household. To do this, we used the [National Statistics Socio-economic Classification (NS-SEC)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/classificationsandstandards/otherclassifications/thenationalstatisticssocioeconomicclassificationnssecrebasedonsoc2010), which groups people based on their occupation.

body.h2: Risk of both neonatal and child death was higher in households with long-term unemployment
body.text: The groups range from those who have never worked or are long-term unemployed, to those in high-paid occupations such as chief executives and company directors.

body.h2: Risk of both neonatal and child death was higher in households with long-term unemployment
body.text: In this analysis, we have compared mortality risk for all socio-economic groups to those in [NS-SEC Class 1](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/classificationsandstandards/otherclassifications/thenationalstatisticssocioeconomicclassificationnssecrebasedonsoc2010#analytic-classes-and-operational-categories), which includes higher managerial and professional jobs. We’ve grouped our cohort based on the NS-SEC classification of the main earner in the household.

body.h2: Risk of both neonatal and child death was higher in households with long-term unemployment
body.text: Babies born into households where the main earner was not in a managerial profession had a higher risk of neonatal death than those in households where the main earner was in a higher managerial or professional job.

body.h2: Risk of both neonatal and child death was higher in households with long-term unemployment
body.text: However, once we accounted for a range of other household and gestational factors (in Model 2), there was no statistical evidence of a higher risk of neonatal death for any socio-economic group.

body.h2: Risk of both neonatal and child death was higher in households with long-term unemployment
body.text: This suggests that the relationship between socio-economic status and neonatal mortality can largely be explained by other factors.

body.box_text:
If you or someone close to you is affected by the issues in this article, you can contact the [Child Bereavement UK](https://www.childbereavementuk.org/) helpline on 0800 02888 40, or [use the live chat function on their website](https://www.childbereavementuk.org/Pages/Category/child-bereavement-uk-support-services).

Child Bereavement UK helps families to rebuild their lives when a child grieves or when a child dies.

You can also contact [The Stillbirth and Neonatal Death Charity (SANDS)](https://www.sands.org.uk/). Sands is there to support anyone affected by pregnancy loss or the death of a baby, however recently or longer ago, for as long as they need this. Find out more: [www.sands.org.uk/support](https://www.sands.org.uk/support-you/how-we-offer-support)

body.h2: Glossary
body.text: Hazard ratio

body.h2: Glossary
body.text: A hazard ratio is a measure of the relative differences in the instantaneous rate of mortality between groups. In short, it is a measure of how often a particular event occur in one group compared to another (reference) group at a given point in time. A hazard ratio greater than one indicates the rate of mortality is higher, and likewise less than one lower, in the population group under study compared with a reference group.

body.h2: Glossary
body.text: Mortality rate per 1000 child-years

body.h2: Glossary
body.text: This is the rate based on deaths and the number of people, for a specified time period. Child-years takes into account both the number of people and follow-up time. This allows us to estimate the number of neonatal and child deaths that would occur among 1,000 individuals per year over our full study period.

body.h2: Glossary
body.text: NS-SEC

body.h2: Glossary
body.text: The [National Statistics Socio-economic classification, or NS-SEC](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/classificationsandstandards/otherclassifications/thenationalstatisticssocioeconomicclassificationnssecrebasedonsoc2010), is a classification system of socio-economic status based on occupations. Further information is available in our [NS-SEC methodology page](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/classificationsandstandards/otherclassifications/thenationalstatisticssocioeconomicclassificationnssecrebasedonsoc2010).

body.h2: Glossary
body.text: In this analysis, we assigned babies and children to a socio-economic group based on the main earner in their household, or household reference person. This could be the person who owns or rents the house they are living in, or the oldest adult in the household, or the highest earner.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Measuring the data

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: This analysis used population level data, linking data from linked birth notifications (2011-2016) to Census 2011 information on mothers’ socio-economic and ethnicity characteristics.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The cohort included in this study included singleton live births born after 24 weeks of pregnancy, to mothers aged at least 12 years at the time of birth.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Babies whose mother was not a usual resident in England or Wales at the time of the 2011 Census were excluded. Stillbirths were also excluded from our cohort.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: These babies were followed-up until December 2021, to a maximum of 10 years of age.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The number of deaths reported in this article and the associated data tables are rounded to the nearest five.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The statistical model used to estimate mortality risk by ethnicity and socio-economic status is called Cox proportional hazards, and these results were expressed in hazard ratios.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The full analysis included 5 models which is detailed in the Data.
